The Bridgestone dates come from the Akao and All About Lean histories; the Lean Enterprise Institute and Wikipedia pages give no dates. The term 社長診断 for the yearly review is the human's own, from years of working in Japanese; English sources call it the president's diagnosis.

docs.title: Intake, planning & deferred
docs.text:
The formal path — brainstorm, spec, epic, tasks — is the preferred on-ramp, but most work does not arrive that way. It arrives as a dog-walk epiphany, a "we should probably…", an "oh, don't forget." Intake is the lossless net: it turns raw input into a tracked issue with near-zero friction, so nothing is lost before it can be planned.

Capturing the seed of an idea when it is fresh is more valuable than planning it out on the spot. Intake optimizes for that.

docs.title: Every issue belongs to an epic
docs.text:
The net is not an exception to the model — it is part of it. In every managed repository, every issue is either a legitimate top-level kind (an epic, a per-quarter archive bucket, or a release tracking issue) or has an epic parent. There is no opt-out and no "unlinked" state, and that includes a half-formed idea captured thirty seconds ago.

What makes that workable is that the parent is the state. An issue's parent epic says where it stands, so no label has to restate it:

State Parent Buildable? Intake — captured, not yet reviewed the intake epic no Planning — judged to need a full epic the planning epic no Deferred — evaluated, but waiting on something before it can move the deferred epic no Ready — a one-off, or part of a planned initiative a repository's ad-hoc epic, a finite epic, or a proxy epic yes

Work moves intake → planning → ready. An item that has been evaluated but cannot move yet — it waits on an upstream release, another issue, a date, or capacity — steps aside into the deferred queue until its revival conditions are met. Only ready work can be built: the pull-request tooling refuses an issue that still sits in the intake, planning or deferred queue, and says which step to take first.

docs.title: The standing queues
docs.text:
The three queues are standing epics — perpetual, like a repository's ad-hoc epic: created once, reused, never auto-closed. Epic (intake): <name> holds captured, unreviewed items; Epic (planning): <name> holds items waiting for (or undergoing) epic creation; Epic (deferred): <name> holds evaluated items parked until their revival conditions are met.

There is one set per queue home. Every public repository shares the org's set in .github, so the whole org-wide queue is one view rather than something scattered across repositories. A private repository keeps its own set, so private work never surfaces in a public issue. Closed items drain into per-quarter archive buckets, so the live queues show only open work.

docs.title: The lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Capture. The moment something is worth remembering, it becomes an intake item — filed already linked under the intake epic. A one-line "don't forget X" is valid, and there is no category to choose: a bug, a spark, and an investigation all enter the same way. No planning, no scoping; that is deliberately deferred.
  2. Review. On a periodic pass, intake is reviewed oldest first, in small batches. For each item the agent checks its current state and recommends a route; the human confirms the batch. There are five routes:
  3. Drop — close it with a reason (not planned). It stays searchable.
  4. Defer — move it into the deferred queue, recording why it waits and what to check before it can come back.
  5. One-off — move it into its target repository as a ready task under that repository's ad-hoc epic (or a named epic). The ad-hoc epic takes only standalone work: an item that is work of a development epic in another org goes under that epic's proxy in the target repository's org, never ad-hoc, and one in the primary's own org goes under the primary itself. A one-off never goes under the hoshin epic: only /vergil:hoshin files its tasks.
  6. Split — replace it with several ready tasks and close it.
  7. Planning — it needs a real design, so it moves to the planning queue, with an estimated epic size.
  8. Plan. A planning review keeps the planning queue correct, oldest first: each item is left (most are), deferred, dropped, or, unusually, sent out as a one-off, to a repository's ad-hoc epic or, for another org's epic, to its proxy, by the same rule as from intake. It never picks. The human chooses what to plan next and runs epic-create on it, picking only what will be implemented soon, since a plan left sitting goes stale. A planning item is the record of its own epic creation: epic-create always works through one, and leaves progress comments so a session can pause and resume days later. A planning item is waiting, in progress, or completed — closed as "planned as" the epic it became, or with the reason it is not worth doing.

A planning item can carry an estimated epic size: S (1–9 tasks), M (10–19), L (20–39) or XL (40+), derived from an estimated task count. Sizing is optional: an item stays unsized (? in vrg-queue) until it is sized. A size is recorded as an epic-size:<S|M|L|XL> label and a dated Sized … comment, both written by vrg-intake-route: an item is sized as it is routed to planning, and the planning review sizes any waiting item still unsized. Deferred items can carry a size too, and a one-off clears it. The size is there so the planning queue can be sorted and filtered by it: vrg-queue planning --sort size --size S lists the small items, oldest first, so small epics need not wait behind large ones. An item whose sizing is in error (!) is always listed too, whatever the filter. 4. Revisit. A deferred item is never forgotten, because every deferral records a reason and the conditions to check (Revisit when:). On a periodic deferred review, the agent actually checks each item's conditions against their real sources — a release page, an issue's state, a date — and recommends one outcome: keep it (not yet), refresh its record, revive it (back to intake, to planning, or as a one-off), or drop it. Only an item in a queue or an ad-hoc epic can be deferred; a task in a finite epic cannot, since parking one task would in effect suspend its whole epic.

A security item — the neutral issue half of a security record — is routed like any other and keeps its advisory links through every move: every advisory it names is retargeted when the item is transferred or recreated, and its one advisory is retargeted when it is split. A split of an item naming several advisories is refused, since which advisory goes to which task can't be inferred; retarget each by hand, one at a time, with vrg-security-record retarget <GHSA> --from <item> --to <task> [--to …], then split. The --to set is the complete set the advisory tracks afterwards: a --to for each task that fixes it and for every other open issue it still tracks, since retarget refuses a set that leaves one out and prints the command that would succeed. See vergil-tooling's Security Records guide.

The intake and planning queues are meant to stay drained: a growing one is a signal to review it, not a place for work to live. The deferred queue is not drained but re-checked — an item stays there exactly as long as its revival conditions are unmet.

docs.title: Nothing escapes
docs.text:
Issues created outside the sanctioned tools — in the web UI, by a script — are healed, not rejected. A daily sweep attaches every orphan it finds to its home's intake epic, so it surfaces at the next review instead of drifting unseen. Placement stays the reviewer's job; the sweep only guarantees that nothing is lost.

The former triage / idea / research kind labels are retired — the parent carries the state now, and the sweep strips the old labels.

docs.title: Visibility changes go one way
docs.text: Because a private repository keeps its own queues and epics, a repository's visibility decides where its work is tracked. Private → public is supported: the sweep moves the repository's open queue items under the org's .github queues, and its epics are relocated to match. Public → private is not supported — work already tracked in public cannot be made private again, so the path is to create a new private repository and migrate the code into it. The audit reports private-repository issues found under public epics for a human to resolve.

docs.title: Mechanics
docs.text: The commands and their exact behavior — vrg-intake-create, vrg-intake-route, vrg-queue, the deferral record, the orphan pass, and the queue-home rules — are documented in vergil-tooling's GitHub Issue Standards (see The deferred queue for deferring and reviving, and Viewing the queues for epic sizes), the CLI reference, and the Epic home visibility flips guide.

docs.title: Tools & skills
docs.text:
The Management layer is operated through two surfaces:

  • vrg-* command-line tools — the mechanical operations (create an epic, link a task, run the audit), maintained in vergil-tooling.
  • Skills — the agent-facing workflows that compose those tools into a process (orchestrate an epic, capture intake, review the queue), maintained in the Claude Code plugin, vergil-claude-plugin.

This page explains how they fit together and who drives what. The dry, per-command reference — every flag of every tool — lives in the repositories where the code does; this is the story, not the man page. For the issue model's mechanics, see vergil-tooling's GitHub Issue Standards.

docs.title: Who drives what
docs.text:
The dividing line is accountability. The speed limit is human comprehension, not code generation — so agents do the development, and humans own the irreversible, outward-facing steps.

Driven by the agent (runs as the user identity) Driven by the human Participating in the brainstorm; running the design-review rounds The judgment calls in the brainstorm, and the decision on each design-review finding and each further round Authoring specs and plans; implementing tasks Submitting the pull request (vrg-submit-pr), which turns GitHub auto-merge on Commits and PR preparation / hand-off Reviewing the change before submitting it: the submit is the decision to merge Read-only audits and dry-runs Settling develop once the PRs merge (vrg-finalize-pr, which the submit runs unless --no-finalize) Filing intake, epics, tasks, links Write-gated ops: migration --apply, audit --close Implementing a dependency-update fix task Releases (vrg-release) and dependency updates (vrg-update-deps) Requesting a review decision, drafting the human's reply and reading it (vrg-ruling) Replying to a review-decision request, as themselves (vrg-ruling-reply)

An agent never merges and never opens a PR itself: it prepares the change and hands off, and a human takes it across the line.

docs.title: Authoring & structure
docs.text:
• vrg-epic-create (mint an epic in .github; with --proxy-for <primary ref> --repo <owner>/<repo> it instead finds, reopens or creates the proxy epic for a primary in another org, in the target's org .github, with its Proxy: comment on the primary)
  • vrg-adhoc-epic (ensure a repo's ad-hoc epic exists)
  • vrg-issue-create (create a task, born linked under an epic)

  • vrg-epic-link / vrg-epic-move (manage the epic↔task relationship)

  • vrg-issue-create --epic adhoc|intake|planning|hoshin (target a repository's standing epic by name rather than by number; hoshin is the org's hoshin epic in <org>/.github, for /vergil:hoshin's logbook tasks)

docs.title: Intake, planning & deferred
docs.text:
• vrg-intake-create (capture an intake item, linked under its home's intake epic as it is created — no category to choose)
  • vrg-intake-route (apply a review's route: drop, defer, one-off, split, or planning out of intake; defer or drop out of planning; and out of deferred, revive to intake, planning or one-off, refresh, drop, or split. Defer requires --reason and --revisit-when, and is the only way into or out of the deferred queue. size --tasks N --reason TEXT records a planning or deferred item's estimated epic size (an epic-size:<S|M|L|XL> label and a dated Sized … comment), planning --tasks N --reason TEXT sizes an item as it enters planning, and a one-off clears the size. A security item keeps its advisory links when it is transferred, recreated, or split; a split of an item naming several advisories is refused)
  • vrg-queue intake|planning|deferred (the read-only view of one queue — intake oldest first, deferred least recently deferred first — or of all three with a bare vrg-queue; a planning item is held at in-progress, never shown as ready-to-close, while any security advisory still tracks it, or while it is security-labelled and names an advisory that cannot be read, until each advisory is retargeted to the task or tasks that fix it. Planning and deferred lines show each item's epic size (M/14, ? unsized, ! in error), and vrg-queue planning also takes --sort age|size|tasks and --size LIST to order and filter by it. An item whose sizing is in error makes the run exit 2, after the full listing (exit 1 is a queue that could not be read or a usage error). See the vrg-intake-route and vrg-queue reference)
  • vrg-queue adhoc (the read-only view of the ready one-off work: the open tasks under every live ad-hoc epic, grouped by repository and oldest first within each, each with its state — ready, blocked by an open Blocked-by: dependency, or in-flight with the marks that show it, such as an open PR, a report-ready record, a feature branch, a worktree or a merge-review directory. --repo narrows it to one repository's ad-hoc epic. It is not a review queue, so it is shown only when named, never by a bare vrg-queue)
  • vrg-queue hoshin (the same read-only view of the open tasks under the org's hoshin epic; --repo narrows it to one repository's tasks. Like adhoc, it is shown only when named)
  • vrg-security-record (record a security finding as a private draft advisory in <org>/.github, paired with a neutral security-labelled intake issue; create, list, show, retarget (move an advisory's tracking to the tasks that fix it; when they are all in another org, the advisory moves to that org's .github), close (close a draft advisory with a reason posted on every issue it tracks), note (append a dated note to an advisory) and sync (the security-records pass: sync each advisory's state to its issues and report broken pairs, run by the human or the user agent, never on a schedule) — see vergil-tooling's Security Records guide)

An issue still in the intake, planning or deferred queue is not buildable: vrg-pr-workflow report-ready and vrg-submit-pr refuse it until it is routed out.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
• vrg-epic-rollup (close a finite epic when its last task closes — event-driven)
  • vrg-finalize-pr (watch the submitted PRs merge, then settle develop once: sync, cleanup, validate and a CD report; it never merges — human, run by vrg-submit-pr by default)

docs.title: Reporting & enforcement
docs.text:
• vrg-roadmap (the open-epic roadmap)
  • vrg-epic-audit (drift and invariant violations — read-only, with a gated --close; under --close, run daily by the scheduled sweep, it also runs the orphan pass that attaches every unparented issue to its home's intake epic. --close makes no security-advisory call: the security-records pass is vrg-security-record sync, which the read-only vrg-epic-audit only previews)

To relocate a finite epic into its correct home (.github), move the issue with vrg-gh issue transfer and re-link its tasks with vrg-epic-link.

docs.title: Pull-request flow
docs.text:
• vrg-commit (standards-compliant commits)
  • vrg-pr-workflow report-ready (records the PR hand-off)
  • vrg-submit-pr (open the PRs against develop with auto-merge on — squash for one issue, rebase for a batch — then finalize them, unless --no-finalize; human-run)

docs.title: Merge review
docs.text:
The merge-review skill's tools, run by the agent between a green vrg-validate and report-ready:

  • vrg-merge-review-request (build a review or check request in the task's private directory; it refuses unless the last vrg-validate was a full, clean, green run at HEAD)
  • vrg-merge-review-check (check a stored reviewer result against its request; the skill acts only on a result that passes)

The request builder decides the change class itself, docs-only or code; a docs-only change is reviewed only for merge quality. vrg-change-class is not part of the loop: it prints the class a branch will get, for humans and debugging.

A repository lists its documentation paths for the change class in the [merge-review] docs-paths key of vergil.toml, read as committed at the branch's merge base. The loop, the records and these tools are in vergil-tooling's Merge Review guide.

docs.title: Review decisions
docs.text:
When a review of a task's change needs the human's decision, the decision travels as an authenticated comment on the task issue:

  • vrg-ruling (the agent's side, run as the user identity: request posts a review-decision request, draft relays the reply it drafts for the human, read reads the human's reply with turn checks, and respond posts the response)
  • vrg-ruling-reply (post the human's reply to a request, as the human — human-run in the human's own shell, like vrg-submit-pr)

The merge-review skill sends every stop for the human through them, and epic-implement drafts the human's replies to those stops. The protocol, its checks and recovery are in vergil-tooling's Human Replies guide.

docs.title: Release
docs.text:
• vrg-release (cut a release from develop to main — human-run)
  • vrg-update-deps (the mechanized dependency update — human-run)

A release ends with an update-deps stage, which runs vrg-update-deps once the release is tagged and published. When anything changed, it opens a deps/update-<next> pull request labelled dependency-update, and a green one is merged. If validation or the merge fails, the PR stays open and a fix task is filed. If an updater itself fails, nothing is pushed and the failure is recorded on the release's tracking issue. Any open dependency-update PR blocks the next release, until its fix task closes as completed — the next vrg-release then closes the PR and the gate clears. Two flags change this: --allow-pending-deps lets an urgent release through despite an open PR, and the bypass is logged on the release's tracking issue; --without-deps skips the update-deps stage. The release procedure itself is in vergil-tooling's Releasing guide.

The vrg-gh and vrg-git wrappers sit under all of this, enforcing the allow-lists and selecting the right identity; raw git/gh are blocked in agent sessions.

docs.title: The skills, by role
docs.text:
• epic-create — the outer orchestrator of the workflow: brainstorm → epic → spec → spec pushback rounds → human spec review → plan → plan pushback rounds → alignment rounds → docs PR → file tasks, always worked through a planning item that records its progress. Its design-review rounds need paad's unattended runner, paad:paad-delegate, which every box, Lima or cloud, gets by installing paad from the vergil fork through the ordinary plugin refresh. A session without it is on a misconfigured box and runs no review round: epic-create stops and tells the human how to fix the box (paad usage policy §10; paad review rounds: what a session needs).
  • intake-capture — the lossless net: file an intake item with near-zero friction.
  • epic-review — the periodic pass over one queue, in small batches, with a mode per queue:
  • epic-review intake works the intake queue oldest first and routes each item out of it: drop, defer, one-off, split, or planning, or leaves it for now. An item routed to planning is always sized as it moves.
  • epic-review planning keeps the planning queue correct, oldest first: each item is left (most are), deferred, dropped, or, unusually, sent to a repo's ad-hoc epic as a one-off. It prunes and never picks: the human chooses what to plan next and runs epic-create on it. It recommends a size for each waiting item that is unsized or in error, and ends by listing the surviving queue, by size when the human asks.
  • epic-review deferred checks each deferred item's Revisit when: conditions against their real sources and recommends keep, refresh, revive, or drop; an unsized item revived to planning is sized as it moves.
  • epic-implement — the driver above the issue-* skills, run as often as needed between epic-create and epic-retrospective. On the development path it resumes an epic from its issue and plan, dispatches every runnable task to issue-implement, issue-validate or issue-deploy (in parallel sub-agents where that helps, batching small independent code tasks), brings everything that needs the human to one gate, and stops. Its adhoc mode works the ad-hoc tasks instead: org-wide with /vergil:epic-implement adhoc, or for one repository with adhoc --repo <owner>/<repo> or that repository's ad-hoc epic ref. On a development epic it also works the tasks of every proxy epic the epic has in another org. It refuses an epic it does not drive and says what does: given an intake, planning or deferred queue it points to epic-review, which is how a queue is worked; given the hoshin epic, to /vergil:hoshin; and given a proxy epic, to its primary (epic-implement).
  • issue-implement — the agent implements a single issue end-to-end, validates it to green, runs merge-review and hands the PR off with the merge review's eligibility line in its notes, in a Lima or a cloud session alike (issue-implement).
  • merge-review — the pre-PR judgement check issue-implement runs once validation is green: one review by the read-only merge-reviewer agent, at most one fix and check, every stop for the human through vrg-ruling, every raised item closed before hand-off, and an eligibility line for the PR notes (merge-review).
  • fixture-run — files a fixture run on one or more of the language fixture repos: per fixture, a change, release and validation trio, blocked by the release or deployment task passed as --after. It files the tasks and never runs them. An epic whose plan changes language support, container images, shared CI workflows or release tooling seeds one run per affected fixture (fixture-run).
  • pr-watch — the agent monitors an open PR through CI and review, reconciling until it is mergeable.

Together, the tools give the mechanical guarantees and the skills give the process on top of them — which is exactly why the story belongs here, in one place, while each tool's and action's mechanical detail stays in its own repo.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text: Getting an idea into shipped, closed tasks is a pipeline — and the whole bet is that front-loading the analysis makes the implementation near-bulletproof. Hours spent up front on design and planning pay for themselves when the pull requests just work the first time.

docs.title: epic-create is the entry point
docs.text:
For non-trivial work, the starting move is epic-create, not brainstorming directly. A solution worth thinking through is worth recording as work, so there is little value in designing something and then walking away from it untracked. epic-create opens into brainstorming and orchestrates the whole sequence. If the design collapses to a trivial, single-PR change, it is a task, not an epic — filed under the target repository's ad-hoc epic, and done.

Every run is tracked in a planning item — an issue in the planning queue that records its own epic creation, with progress comments so a session can pause and resume days later:

  • epic-create <issue> starts or resumes that planning item (an intake or deferred item is first moved to the planning queue).
  • epic-create with a free-text idea first turns the idea into a new planning item.
  • epic-create with no argument summarizes the planning queue and asks which item to work on.

Choosing which item to plan next is the human's act: they pick it and run epic-create on it, picking only what will be implemented soon, since a plan left sitting goes stale. epic-review planning does not choose; it keeps the planning queue correct. Each item that is still valid stays, and the rest are deferred, dropped or, unusually, sent to a repo's ad-hoc epic as a one-off. The pass ends by listing the surviving queue to help the human choose. A planning item can carry an estimated epic size (S, M, L or XL). Sizing is optional: an unsized item shows ? in vrg-queue. For the small-end cadence, vrg-queue planning --sort size --size S lists the small items (an estimated 1–9 tasks), oldest first, and any item whose sizing is in error (!), which is always listed whatever the filter.

The planning item closes once the epic exists, its docs task has merged, and its tasks are filed — "planned as" the epic it became.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
epic-create drives these stages in order:

  1. Brainstorm — explore intent and converge on an approved design.
  2. Initialize — create the epic in .github and seed its bookend tasks (documentation first; documentation review and the retrospective last).
  3. Spec → spec pushback rounds → human review — write the spec, critique it adversarially in spec pushback rounds, and have a human review it.
  4. Plan → plan pushback rounds → alignment rounds — write the implementation plan in one automated pass, critique it in plan pushback rounds, then reconcile the spec and the plan in alignment rounds, which may change both.
  5. Docs PR — land the spec and plan as a single documentation PR (which closes the documentation bookend).
  6. File tasks — create the implementation tasks from the plan, each in the repository where its PR will land.

The review steps in stages 3 and 4 run in human-gated rounds, described below.

docs.title: The interaction doctrine
docs.text:
The design and review steps are not hand-waving — each runs a concrete, reusable skill, composed from two packages: Superpowers (brainstorming, writing-plans) and PAAD (pushback, alignment). Brainstorming produces the spec, pushback critiques the spec, writing-plans generates the plan, pushback critiques the plan, and alignment confirms the spec and the plan match. The pipeline mixes interactive, human-gated and automated stages on purpose:

Stage Mode Contract superpowers:brainstorming interactive Explore intent, one question at a time — produces the spec. Design review (pushback on the spec, pushback on the plan, alignment) human-gated rounds A fresh review-only subagent per round, run by paad's unattended runner. The main session walks the human through the findings, and the human decides every further round. superpowers:writing-plans automated Generate the implementation plan in one pass; no gating.

Each design-review round reviews the whole document, and the main session records it as a comment on the planning item. The human decides every finding and whether to run another round of the stage. The rules are in the paad review doctrine, mode 1. How the workflow uses PAAD, and every place it deviates from the PAAD authors' recommendations, is recorded in the paad usage policy.

Every design-review round needs paad's unattended runner, paad:paad-delegate. Every box, the host, Lima VMs and cloud VMs alike, installs paad from the vergil fork through the ordinary plugin refresh, so every session has the delegate. A session without it is on a misconfigured box and runs no review round: epic-create stops and tells the human how to fix the box (paad usage policy §10; doctrine §1.8; paad review rounds: what a session needs).

The human-judgment principle governs brainstorming: stop and ask only for ambiguities or judgment calls that materially affect the outcome; handle minor, obvious corrections by batching them to the end as a single "here are the no-brainers — correct me if I'm wrong" review, rather than gating each one.

Design review walks the findings one at a time, in severity order, except for one batch at the end: low findings, each with its own decision, and known findings, which keep their earlier decision unless the human pulls one out (doctrine §2.2, step 4).

The goal of all this front-loading is blunt: plans that just work — on the order of 90–99% of tasks green on first implementation. Real-world misses still happen and get patched, but the more upfront refinement, the higher the success rate, and the more mechanical work can eventually be forked off and trusted to run on its own.

Each task is then implemented with the issue-implement skill, which implements the issue, validates it to green and hands the PR off to the human. Between a green vrg-validate and the hand-off with report-ready, it runs the merge-review skill: one review of the change by the read-only merge-reviewer agent, at most one fix and a check of that fix, and every stop for the human through an authenticated vrg-ruling request on the task issue. Its eligibility line goes into the PR notes. The detail is in vergil-tooling's Merge Review guide.

Given a list of small issues of one epic in one repository, issue-implement implements them as one batch: one branch, one commit per issue, each issue validated and merge-reviewed on its own, and one hand-off that becomes one PR with a Closes line per issue. epic-implement may batch independent small ready tasks the same way. What may be batched, and how a batch is stopped or resumed, is in the plugin's issue-implement reference and the skill's Batch mode section.

Merge review is not paad: issue-implement runs no paad review of its own, so it works the same in a Lima or a cloud session; paad's review rounds belong to design review in epic-create.

docs.title: Working the ad-hoc tasks
docs.text:
Not every ready task belongs to a planned epic: a one-off routed out of a queue, or a design that collapsed to a single PR, is a task under its repository's ad-hoc epic. Those tasks are worked with epic-implement in its adhoc mode — org-wide with /vergil:epic-implement adhoc, or for one repository with adhoc --repo <owner>/<repo> or that repository's ad-hoc epic ref.

Ad-hoc tasks are standalone work only, each picked up, merged and released on its own. Two kinds of ready task that are not standalone have homes of their own, and epic-implement refuses both epics:

  • Hoshin's logbook tasks sit under the org's hoshin epic. Given it, epic-implement stops and points to /vergil:hoshin, which files and works them.

  • Another org's epic tasks sit under that epic's proxy. Given a proxy, epic-implement stops and points to its primary: running it on the primary works the proxy's tasks beside the primary's own.

  • Collect. It gathers the open tasks under the ad-hoc epics with vrg-queue adhoc and summarizes them by repository. A task already handed off or worked elsewhere (an open PR, a report-ready record, a remote branch) is left alone; one that stopped on this machine is resumed the way the development path resumes a task.

  • Propose a strategy. There is no plan to set an order, so it proposes one: which tasks to batch together per repository, which to run alone, which to leave for later, and the order, oldest first unless there is a reason to differ. Ad-hoc tasks are filed one at a time and rarely say what they depend on, so the strategy judges overlap explicitly — tasks that touch the same files are batched or run one after another — and names which tasks run at the same time.
  • One confirmation. The human confirms the whole strategy once.
  • Dispatch and gate. It dispatches the tasks under the same gates, ruling relay and batching rules as a development epic, brings everything that needs the human to one gate, and stops. Its records go on the ad-hoc epic of the repository concerned.

The adhoc mode reads no plan and drafts no retrospective: an ad-hoc epic has no plan and never closes. Like the development path, it is stateless, so re-running it re-derives where things stand from GitHub.
